summary_vn: Giải thích đám cưới Việt — lễ ăn hỏi, lễ cưới, áo dài, và phong bì mừng — bằng tiếng Anh.
summary_en: Explain Vietnamese weddings — engagement, ceremony, áo dài, and red envelope gifts — in English.
regional_note: Đám cưới miền Bắc và miền Nam khác về thứ tự và quà hồi môn. Miền Bắc giữ nghi lễ truyền thống chặt chẽ hơn; miền Nam linh hoạt hơn về số lượng tráp và lễ vật.

phrases.vn_moment: Hai đám: lễ ăn hỏi và lễ cưới
phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao đi đám cưới hai lần.
phrases.english: There are usually two ceremonies — the engagement ('lễ ăn hỏi') and the wedding day itself. The engagement happens at the bride's family home; the wedding is the big public party.
phrases.cultural_note: If you're invited to both, that's a sign of close friendship or family connection. The engagement is more intimate.

phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao cô dâu mặc áo truyền thống đỏ.
phrases.english: The bride wears 'áo dài' — our traditional long dress. Red is the lucky color for weddings, so the engagement áo dài is usually red. The Western white gown comes out later for the reception.
phrases.cultural_note: Two outfits is the norm: red áo dài for the traditional ceremony, then a Western-style white gown for the reception or evening party.

phrases.context: Đoàn nhà trai đến nhà gái rước dâu.
phrases.english: On the wedding day, the groom's family processes to the bride's house in matching outfits, carrying gifts in red lacquered boxes called 'tráp.' The procession can have eight to twelve attendants.
phrases.cultural_note: The number of trays is symbolic and depends on family agreement. Even numbers in the south, sometimes paired in the north.

phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp hỏi 'cái hộp đỏ' đó là gì.
phrases.english: The red trays carry traditional gifts: betel leaves, areca nuts, tea, fruits, sweets, and roasted pig. Each tray represents a different blessing for the marriage.
phrases.cultural_note: Betel and areca are the most symbolic items — they reference an old folktale about loyalty in marriage. Don't joke about the contents.

phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp được mời đám cưới bạn người Việt và hỏi nên tặng gì.
phrases.english: The standard wedding gift is cash in a red envelope — that's what we expect. Bring the envelope to the door; there's a box for them at the reception.
phrases.cultural_note: Don't bring a physical present — it's not expected and might be awkward to transport. Cash in a red envelope is the right move.

phrases.context: Tư vấn cho bạn không phải người Việt về số tiền mừng.
phrases.english: The amount usually covers your seat — wedding receptions can run to several million đồng per head. A safe rule is what you'd spend on a nice restaurant dinner where you live.
phrases.cultural_note: The cash is partly to help cover costs, but the wish on the envelope matters more than hitting a specific amount.

phrases.context: Cô dâu chú rể rót trà mời họ hàng.
phrases.english: The bride and groom serve tea to each parent and elder one by one. The elder drinks, gives a blessing, and then a small gift — usually jewelry or a red envelope.
phrases.cultural_note: This is a serious moment, not photo-op time. Stand back and let the family go through the order without interrupting for photos.

phrases.context: Giải thích vai trò người mai mối truyền thống.
phrases.english: Some traditional weddings still have a 'bà mối' — a matchmaker or family elder who formally introduces the families and speaks at the engagement. Even in modern matches, an aunt or older relative often plays the role.
phrases.cultural_note: Even when the couple met on their own, having a respected elder make the formal introduction is what makes the engagement feel official.

phrases.context: Bạn không phải người Việt được mời và hỏi cách ngồi.
phrases.english: Reception tables seat ten. There's no plus-one culture by default — you'll be assigned to a table with friends or coworkers of the bride/groom. Show up around the listed time and check the seating chart at the door.
phrases.cultural_note: Plus-ones aren't standard. Don't bring one without asking. Tables fill quickly and rearranging is awkward.

phrases.context: Đối phương ép cạn ly khi chúc rượu.
phrases.english: When someone toasts you with '100%' or 'cạn ly,' they want you to drain the glass. It's friendly, not aggressive — but you can decline politely if you don't drink.
phrases.cultural_note: Pressure-drinking culture is real at Vietnamese weddings. Saying 'I don't drink' or 'I'm driving' is fine and respected.

phrases.context: Bạn không phải người Việt hỏi có thể đem con nhỏ không.
phrases.english: Vietnamese weddings are usually all-ages — bringing kids is normal, even welcome. There's no strict 'adults only' rule.
phrases.cultural_note: This often surprises Western friends. Vietnamese weddings are family events, not nightlife events.

phrases.context: Câu chúc kinh điển khi gặp cô dâu chú rể.
phrases.english: The classic wedding wish is 'a hundred years of happiness together' — 'trăm năm hạnh phúc.' We say it in Vietnamese; the literal translation works in English too.
phrases.cultural_note: It's the equivalent weight of 'cheers to a long marriage' in the West. Don't shorten it to a casual 'congrats.'

phrases.vn_moment: Chào bố mẹ cô dâu / chú rể
phrases.context: Khi đến chỗ tiệc gặp bố mẹ hai bên.
phrases.english: When you arrive, look for the bride's and groom's parents — they're usually receiving guests at the entrance. A short handshake and a 'congratulations on the wedding' goes a long way.
phrases.cultural_note: Skipping the parents on the way in reads as poor manners. Don't head straight to your table without greeting them.

phrases.vn_moment: Chụp ảnh cưới trước ngày cưới
phrases.context: Giải thích bộ ảnh chụp ngoài trời trước đám.
phrases.english: Couples shoot a wedding photo album weeks before the actual ceremony — outdoor locations, multiple outfits. The album gets displayed at the reception.
phrases.cultural_note: Pre-wedding photos are standard. Asking 'so were these taken on the day?' is fine — the answer's almost always 'no, weeks ago.'

phrases.context: Lễ đưa cô dâu ra cửa nhà mẹ đẻ.
phrases.english: Traditionally, the bride leaves her parents' house to live with the groom's family. There's a quiet, emotional moment where she says goodbye to her parents at the door.
phrases.cultural_note: Even in modern weddings where the couple moves into their own apartment, this moment is preserved symbolically. It can be tearful — don't crash it for photos.

dialogues.title: Coworker invited to your wedding
dialogues.setting: A coworker received the wedding invitation and isn't sure what to expect.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: Thanks for the invitation! I'm a little nervous — I've never been to a Vietnamese wedding. What should I bring?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Just yourself and a red envelope with cash. That's the standard wedding gift in Vietnamese culture — physical presents aren't expected.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: How much should be in the envelope?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Roughly what you'd spend on a nice restaurant dinner. The number isn't strict — what matters is the wish that goes with it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Something semi-formal — what you'd wear to a Western wedding works. Avoid all-white; that reads as competing with the bride. Red is great for guests, especially for women.

dialogues.title: Friend asks about the engagement ceremony
dialogues.setting: A close friend wants to know why your engagement is a 'whole event.'

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: So why is the engagement a separate party? In the US it's usually just an announcement.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: In Vietnamese tradition, the engagement is the formal moment between the two families. The groom's family processes to the bride's house carrying these red trays of gifts — tea, fruit, betel leaves, sweets — to ask formally for the marriage.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: An older relative speaks on behalf of the groom's family — sometimes called the 'bà mối,' the matchmaker. Even if we met without one, the role still exists at the ceremony.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: And the bride's family says yes there?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Right. After the formal acceptance, the date is set for the actual wedding. So you're invited to two events about a month apart — engagement is smaller, just families and close friends; wedding is the big public party.
